title: How does Object.groupBy() work in ES2024 and when should you use it over reduce?
description: ES2024 added Object.groupBy to natively group iterables. Understand its callback, return shape, and why it replaces the classic reduce boilerplate.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Iterable</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">[item, item, ...]</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">groupBy(fn)</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">(el, i) => key</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">{ key: [...] }</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">null prototype</text></svg>

**Core concept.** Object.groupBy(iterable, callback) groups elements by a string/symbol key in one pass and returns a null-prototype object — a native, optimized replacement for the manual reduce grouping pattern.

How it works — Object.groupBy is a static method (like Object.keys) that iterates any iterable, calls callback(element, index) and coerces the return to a property key. Unlike reduce, there is no accumulator to initialize and no risk of prototype pollution because the result is created with null prototype, so keys like "__proto__" or "constructor" are safe. It runs in a single pass and engines can optimize the grouping loop better than userland reduce.

The callback receives the same arguments as Array.prototype.map, so index matters for positional grouping, but the grouping key must be stringifiable — numbers become strings, symbols stay symbols. If you need non-string keys (objects, numbers preserved as numbers), use Map.groupBy instead. Object.groupBy is intentionally for string-keyed plain objects that serialize cleanly to JSON.

A second nuance is ordering: groups appear in insertion order of first occurrence of each key, and values within each group preserve original iteration order. That makes it deterministic for UI rendering and tests, unlike hand-rolled reduce where ordering depends on implementation.

| | Before (reduce) | After (Object.groupBy) |
|---|---|---|
| Boilerplate | 5-6 lines, init {} | 1 line |
| Prototype safety | Pollutable if key is __proto__ | null-proto, safe |
| Key types | Any coerced, risky | String/symbol only (use Map.groupBy for objects) |
| Performance | Userland loop | Engine-optimized grouping |

> **Interview tip:** If asked to group by property, write Object.groupBy(items, x => x.category) then mention Map.groupBy for non-string keys. Interviewers award points for naming the null-prototype safety.

```js
const products = [
  { name: 'apple', type: 'fruit' },
  { name: 'carrot', type: 'veg' },
  { name: 'banana', type: 'fruit' }
];

// native
const byType = Object.groupBy(products, p => p.type);
console.log(byType);
// { fruit: [{name:'apple'}, {name:'banana'}], veg: [{name:'carrot'}] }

// safe with dangerous key
const weird = Object.groupBy(['a','b'], () => '__proto__');
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(weird) === null); // true
console.log(weird['__proto__']); // ['a','b'] — no pollution

// equivalent reduce (verbose, pollutable)
const old = products.reduce((acc, p) => {
  (acc[p.type] ??= []).push(p);
  return acc;
}, {});
```

title: What does Promise.withResolvers() solve and how does it replace the deferred anti-pattern?
description: ES2024 introduced Promise.withResolvers as the standard way to expose resolve/reject outside the executor. Learn why the deferred pattern was problematic and how to use it.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">executor</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">new Promise(()=>{})</text><line class="d-edge" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">withResolvers()</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">{ promise, resolve, reject }</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">External control</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">resolve() anywhere</text></svg>

**Core concept.** Promise.withResolvers() returns { promise, resolve, reject } so you can settle a promise from outside its executor — standardizing the old deferred pattern without closure hacks.

How it works — Before this API developers wrote let resolve; const p = new Promise(r => resolve = r), which is verbose and leaks the resolver through closure capture. withResolvers creates the promise and captures its internal resolve/reject in one atomic operation, returning all three as a plain object. The promise is still a normal Promise — thenable, chainable, and compatible with await — only the control handles are externalized.

This matters for event-driven code: converting callbacks, streams, or WebSocket messages to promises. Instead of nesting logic inside an executor, you create the promise up front, store resolve/reject, and call them from event handlers. It also cleans up async queue patterns where a producer resolves work that a consumer awaits.

Engine-wise it avoids the extra closure allocation of the deferred pattern and makes intent explicit in code review. The method is static, so Promise.withResolvers() reads as a factory, and destructuring makes it ergonomic: const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers().

| | Before (deferred) | After (withResolvers) |
|---|---|---|
| Syntax | let res; new Promise(r=>res=r) | const {promise, resolve}=Promise.withResolvers() |
| Safety | Resolver leaks via closure, easy to forget | Atomic, explicit return value |
| Readability | Intent hidden | Intent clear: external control |

> **Interview tip:** Mention this replaces the jQuery Deferred / manual deferred antipattern. If asked to promisify an event, reach for withResolvers and say you would use it for AbortSignal or iterator bridging.

```js
// before — deferred antipattern
let resolve;
const p1 = new Promise(r => { resolve = r; });
resolve(42);

// after — ES2024
const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers();

// practical: bridge an event to a promise
function onceEvent(target, event) {
  const { promise, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers();
  target.addEventListener(event, resolve, { once: true });
  return promise;
}

// queue example
async function createQueue() {
  let { promise, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers();
  return {
    push(val) { resolve(val); ({ promise, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers()); },
    next() { return promise; }
  };
}
console.log(await Promise.withResolvers().promise.catch(()=> 'never')); // demo shape
```

title: How do Import Attributes (`with { type: "json" }`) work and why did they replace import assertions?
description: The `with` keyword for import attributes is the ES2024+ way to import JSON and other types safely. Understand syntax, security model, and migration from `assert`.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="220" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="130" y="85" text-anchor="middle">import data from</text><text class="d-sub" x="130" y="105" text-anchor="middle">"./data.json"</text><line class="d-edge" x1="240" y1="90" x2="320" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="320,90 310,84 310,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="330" y="40" width="220" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="440" y="85" text-anchor="middle">with { type: "json" }</text><text class="d-sub" x="440" y="105" text-anchor="middle">attribute check</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="550" y1="90" x2="630" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="630,90 620,84 620,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="640" y="40" width="160" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="720" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Parsed JSON</text><text class="d-sub" x="720" y="105" text-anchor="middle">immutable module</text></svg>

**Core concept.** Import Attributes let you annotate an import with with { type: "json" } so the engine knows how to parse the module, replacing the abandoned assert syntax with a forward-compatible attributes model.

How it works — You write import data from "./config.json" with { type: "json" }. The with clause is not a runtime check but a load-time attribute that the host (browser, Node) uses to select the correct loader. If the file is not JSON, the import fails early rather than executing arbitrary code. The imported value is the parsed JSON as the default export, deeply immutable in the module graph.

Import assertions (assert { type: "json" }) were the earlier proposal but assert implied a runtime assertion that could be ignored, while attributes signal semantic metadata the host must respect. Attributes also generalize beyond JSON — future types like css or bytes will use the same with syntax without grammar changes. Old code using assert still works in some bundlers but is deprecated.

Tooling impact: bundlers and TypeScript 5.3+ support with, and Node 20.12+ / 22 treats with as the canonical form. Dynamic import uses the second argument: await import("./data.json", { with: { type: "json" } }). Forgetting the attribute throws a TypeError, which is the security win — it prevents MIME-type confusion attacks where an attacker swaps a JSON file for JS.

| | Before (assert) | After (with) |
|---|---|---|
| Syntax | assert { type: "json" } | with { type: "json" } |
| Semantics | Assertion, ignorable | Attribute, load requirement |
| Extensibility | JSON only | Future types (css, etc.) |
| Tooling | Deprecated warning | Standard, no warning |

> **Interview tip:** Say "assert was renamed to with because attributes are not assertive — they describe the module type, not just check it." Show both static and dynamic import forms.

```js
// static — ES2024+
import config from './config.json' with { type: 'json' };
console.log(config.apiUrl);

// dynamic — note second arg
const data = await import('./data.json', { with: { type: 'json' } });
console.log(data.default.users);

// re-export
export { default as en } from './locales/en.json' with { type: 'json' };

// Node 22 also allows
// import('./x.json', { with: { type: 'json' } }).then(m => m.default)
```

title: How does the Temporal API fix JavaScript Date — Instant, PlainDate and ZonedDateTime?
description: Temporal is the Stage 3 replacement for Date that separates time instants from wall-clock dates. Learn the core types and why Date is broken.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="180" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="110" y="80" text-anchor="middle">Instant</text><text class="d-sub" x="110" y="100" text-anchor="middle">exact ns on timeline</text><text class="d-sub" x="110" y="115" text-anchor="middle">UTC epoch</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="200" y1="90" x2="270" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="270,90 260,84 260,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="280" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="380" y="80" text-anchor="middle">PlainDate / PlainTime</text><text class="d-sub" x="380" y="100" text-anchor="middle">wall-clock, no zone</text><text class="d-sub" x="380" y="115" text-anchor="middle">calendar-aware</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="480" y1="90" x2="550" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="550,90 540,84 540,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="560" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="660" y="80" text-anchor="middle">ZonedDateTime</text><text class="d-sub" x="660" y="100" text-anchor="middle">Instant + zone + cal</text><text class="d-sub" x="660" y="115" text-anchor="middle">DST safe</text></svg>

**Core concept.** Temporal replaces the mutable, zero-indexed Date with immutable types that separate an exact instant (Instant) from human calendar concepts (PlainDate, ZonedDateTime), eliminating DST and timezone bugs.

How it works — Date conflates everything: months are 0-indexed, timezones are implicit, and mutability causes aliasing bugs. Temporal splits concerns: Instant is nanoseconds since Unix epoch in UTC; PlainDate/PlainTime represent wall-clock values without a timezone (birthdays, opening hours); PlainDateTime is wall-clock without zone; ZonedDateTime ties an Instant to a time zone and calendar with DST awareness. All objects are immutable, so with() returns a new instance.

Calendar support is built-in — you can do Temporal.PlainDate.from({ year: 2025, month: 3, day: 15, calendar: 'gregory' }) and arithmetic respects month lengths and calendars beyond Gregorian. Duration arithmetic is explicit: add({ months: 1 }) does calendar-aware math, not fixed 30 days. Parsing uses ISO 8601 with nanosecond precision and never falls back to implementation-dependent Date.parse quirks.

Interoperability needs care: Temporal is polyfilled via @js-temporal/polyfill today; native shipping is in Chrome 120+ behind flag and expected stable in 2025-26. Bridge to Date via Temporal.Instant.fromEpochMilliseconds(Date.now()) and back via instant.epochMilliseconds.

| | Before (Date) | After (Temporal) |
|---|---|---|
| Mutation | Mutable, shared refs bite | Immutable, with() clones |
| Timezone | Implicit, DST bugs | Explicit Plain vs Zoned |
| Precision | Milliseconds | Nanoseconds |
| Calendar | Gregorian only | Pluggable calendars |

> **Interview tip:** Say "Never use Date for scheduling across zones — use ZonedDateTime for events and PlainDate for birthdays." Write a compare showing Date month off-by-one vs Temporal month 1-12.

```js
// polyfill: import { Temporal } from '@js-temporal/polyfill';
const instant = Temporal.Now.instant(); // exact time
console.log(instant.toString()); // 2025-08-26T14:00:00Z

const plain = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2025-02-28');
const next = plain.add({ months: 1 }); // 2025-03-28 (calendar aware)
console.log(next.toString());

const zoned = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from('2025-03-09T01:30:00[America/New_York]');
const later = zoned.add({ hours: 1 }); // DST spring-forward handled
console.log(later.toString()); // 2025-03-09T03:30:00-04:00[America/New_York]

// duration
const d = Temporal.PlainTime.from('09:00').until(Temporal.PlainTime.from('17:30'));
console.log(d.toString()); // PT8H30M
```

title: What does `using` / `await using` do for Explicit Resource Management (ES2024)?
description: The `using` keyword brings RAII-style disposal to JavaScript via Symbol.dispose. Learn how it guarantees cleanup for files, locks, and connections.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">using handle =</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">acquire()</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Scope body</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">use handle</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">[Symbol.dispose]</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">auto on exit</text></svg>

**Core concept.** using declares a disposable resource whose [Symbol.dispose] or [Symbol.asyncDispose] is automatically called when the block scope exits — like try/finally but declarative and exception-safe.

How it works — A resource implements [Symbol.dispose]() or [Symbol.asyncDispose](). Writing using file = openFile() binds the resource to the current block; when control leaves (return, throw, or normal exit) the engine calls file[Symbol.dispose]() in reverse declaration order (LIFO), mirroring C# using and C++ RAII. await using does the same but awaits async dispose, required for async cleanup like closing DB connections.

Scope is block-level, not function-level, so you can scope precisely inside if or for blocks. Multiple using declarations in one line dispose in reverse order, enabling nested locks: using a = lock(), b = lock() — b disposes before a. Errors during disposal are aggregated via SuppressedError (ES2024), so an exception in the body and one in dispose both surface, unlike a naive finally that would swallow the first.

This eliminates forgotten close() calls and pairs well with new APIs like FileHandle and custom connection pools. It only works with explicit using — const and let do not dispose, making intent visible in review. For sync disposable, dispose runs synchronously; for await using you must be inside an async function or async block.

| | Before (try/finally) | After (using) |
|---|---|---|
| Cleanup | Manual finally, easy to forget | Automatic on scope exit |
| Async | try/finally + await close() | await using + asyncDispose |
| Error handling | Later error masks earlier | SuppressedError preserves both |
| Order | Manual nesting | LIFO automatic |

> **Interview tip:** Mention LIFO order and SuppressedError — interviewers test that dispose still runs on throw. Show a custom DisposableStack for managing multiple resources conditionally.

```js
// sync disposable
{
  using file = {
    data: 'hello',
    [Symbol.dispose]() { console.log('closed'); }
  };
  console.log(file.data);
} // -> closed (even if throw)

// async disposable
async function withDb() {
  await using conn = {
    async [Symbol.asyncDispose]() { console.log('db closed'); }
  };
  console.log('query');
} // await disposes after block

// managing multiple manually
{
  const stack = new DisposableStack();
  const h1 = stack.use({ [Symbol.dispose](){ console.log('h1'); }});
  const h2 = stack.use({ [Symbol.dispose](){ console.log('h2'); }});
  // disposes h2 then h1 on scope exit if you use stack
}
```

title: What is `scheduler.yield()` and how does it prevent main-thread blocking?
description: scheduler.yield is the new cooperative scheduling primitive for breaking up long tasks without resorting to setTimeout(0). Understand priorities and browser support.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Long task</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">50ms+ blocking</text><line class="d-edge" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">await scheduler.yield()</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">yield to browser</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Paint + input</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">resume later</text></svg>

**Core concept.** scheduler.yield() is an async yield point that lets the browser paint and handle input mid-task, solving the "long task" INP problem cooperatively without setTimeout hacks.

How it works — Long synchronous loops block rendering and make INP and TBT explode. Before yield, developers sliced work with setTimeout(0) or postTask, but those have clamped delays and lose priority/continuation semantics. scheduler.yield() returns a Promise that resolves as soon as the browser has had a chance to run rendering and higher-priority work, then resumes the same task with its original priority. It is part of the Prioritized Task Scheduling API (scheduler.postTask / scheduler.yield).

Because it is await-able, you place await scheduler.yield() inside a for loop chunk. The scheduler preserves task continuity — unlike setTimeout — so signal priority and task attribution stay intact, which matters for scheduler.postTask priorities (user-blocking, user-visible, background). Yield is cooperative, not preemptive; you still decide where to break.

Browser-wise, scheduler.yield is shipping in Chromium 115+; polyfill is await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0)) but with worse semantics. For React, this complements startTransition and should not replace it for state updates — yield is for imperative work like parsing large JSON or canvas processing.

| | Before (setTimeout 0) | After (scheduler.yield) |
|---|---|---|
| Delay | Clamped ~4ms, loses priority | Immediate yield, preserves priority |
| Semantics | New macrotask, new identity | Continuation of same task |
| INP | Partial help, janky | Explicit yield points, smooth |
| Stack trace | Breaks | Maintained via scheduler |

> **Interview tip:** If asked how to keep a 100k row processing from janking, answer "chunk with for loop + if (i % 100 === 0) await scheduler.yield()" and mention you would measure with Long Tasks API or INP.

```js
// yield inside a heavy loop
async function processItems(items) {
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    heavyWork(items[i]);
    if (i % 100 === 0) {
      // let browser paint & handle input
      await scheduler.yield();
    }
  }
}

// polyfill fallback
const yieldPoly = () => (globalThis.scheduler?.yield
  ? scheduler.yield()
  : new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0)));

// with postTask priority
async function prioritized() {
  await scheduler.postTask(() => console.log('high'), { priority: 'user-blocking' });
  await scheduler.yield(); // resume after paint
}
```

title: How does ArrayBuffer transfer and detach work with `transfer()` vs `transferToFixedLength()`?
description: ES2024 made ArrayBuffer transfer explicit and resizable-aware. Learn zero-copy ownership transfer, detached buffers, and why structuredClone needs it.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">ArrayBuffer</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">8 bytes, owned</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">buffer.transfer()</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">move ownership</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box-muted" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Original: detached</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">byteLength 0</text></svg>

**Core concept.** ArrayBuffer.prototype.transfer() moves ownership of the backing memory to a new buffer and detaches the original (byteLength 0), enabling zero-copy handoff without copying bytes.

How it works — Transfer is a linear ownership move: the new buffer gets the same memory block, the old buffer becomes detached — any view on it throws TypeError. This is cheaper than slice() which copies. ES2024 split transfer into transfer() (retains resizable nature, grows with original maxByteLength) and transferToFixedLength() which strips resizability and optionally truncates/pads to a new length. Before these methods, transfer only happened implicitly via postMessage transfer list, which was easy to misuse.

Resizable ArrayBuffers add nuance: const buf = new ArrayBuffer(8, { maxByteLength: 16 }) creates a growable buffer. buf.transfer() preserves maxByteLength; buf.transferToFixedLength(4) returns a fixed 4-byte copy and detaches the source. Checking buf.detached or catching on access tells you if transfer happened. SharedArrayBuffer cannot be transferred, only shared.

Use cases are workers and high-performance I/O: move a 100 MB buffer to a worker without copy, or steal an ImageData buffer after processing to avoid holding two copies in memory.

| | Before (slice / postMessage list) | After (transfer) |
|---|---|---|
| Copy | Copies bytes, 2x memory | Zero-copy move |
| Detach | Only via postMessage second arg | Explicit buffer.transfer() |
| Resizable | Not preserved correctly | transfer() vs transferToFixedLength() |
| Safety | Easy to forget detached check | .detached property + explicit API |

> **Interview tip:** Say "transfer detaches — any TypedArray view becomes unusable" and mention you must not read byteLength without try/catch after transfer. If asked about resizable buffers, name both methods.

```js
const buf = new ArrayBuffer(8);
const view = new Uint8Array(buf);
view[0] = 42;

const buf2 = buf.transfer(); // moves memory
console.log(buf.detached); // true
console.log(buf.byteLength); // 0
console.log(buf2.byteLength); // 8
try { console.log(view[0]); } catch(e) { console.log('detached view', e.message); }

// fixed-length truncate
const buf3 = new ArrayBuffer(8, { maxByteLength: 16 });
const fixed = buf3.transferToFixedLength(4);
console.log(fixed.byteLength, fixed.resizable); // 4 false

// old postMessage style (still valid)
const worker = new Worker(URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([''])));
const b = new ArrayBuffer(4);
// worker.postMessage(b, [b]); // transfers, b becomes detached
```

title: What is `Array.fromAsync()` and how does it handle async iterables differently from `Array.from()`?
description: Array.fromAsync is the async counterpart to Array.from for iterables that yield promises. Understand buffering, ordering, and mapping with await.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Async Iterable</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">yield promise</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Array.fromAsync</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">await each + mapFn</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Array</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">preserved order</text></svg>

**Core concept.** Array.fromAsync(asyncIterable, mapFn?) awaits each element (including promises) and returns a Promise for the final array, preserving iteration order unlike Promise.all.

How it works — Array.from() only works for sync iterables; given an async iterable it would push promise objects, not resolved values. fromAsync iterates using for await...of under the hood, awaiting each next() result and each yielded value if it is a promise. The optional mapFn can be async as well — fromAsync awaits its return before placing the element, so ordering is deterministic even if mapping is async.

Two overloads: if the input is a sync iterable, fromAsync still wraps each value with await and returns a Promise<Array>. If it is an async iterable, it consumes it to completion. Error handling rejects the returned promise on first iteration error or if mapFn throws/rejects.

Practical wins: consuming paginated APIs that expose [Symbol.asyncIterator], reading Node readable streams, or mapping over an async generator without manual push loops. Contrast with Promise.all(items.map(fn)) which expects an already-materialized array and runs all promises concurrently; fromAsync streams sequentially in iterator order.

| | Before (Array.from / manual) | After (Array.fromAsync) |
|---|---|---|
| Async iterable | Returns [Promise, Promise] | Awaits and returns [value, value] |
| Async map | Need Promise.all after map | Built-in await mapFn |
| Order | Manual handling | Guaranteed iteration order |
| API | for await + push loop | One-liner |

> **Interview tip:** Say "fromAsync is for iterables that produce promises; Promise.all is for arrays that already contain promises." Mention it is the only built-in that consumes an async iterable into an array.

```js
async function* gen() {
  yield 1;
  yield Promise.resolve(2);
  yield 3;
}

const arr = await Array.fromAsync(gen());
console.log(arr); // [1,2,3] — not [1, Promise, 3]

// async mapFn — awaited sequentially in order
const doubled = await Array.fromAsync(gen(), async x => {
  await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 10));
  return x * 2;
});
console.log(doubled); // [2,4,6]

// sync iterable still works (returns Promise)
const fromSync = await Array.fromAsync([1,2,3], x => x * 10);
console.log(fromSync); // [10,20,30]

// consuming a paginated async iterable
async function* pages(fetchPage) {
  let page = 0;
  while (true) {
    const data = await fetchPage(page++);
    if (!data.length) break;
    yield* data;
  }
}
```

title: What is the difference between `Object.groupBy()` and `Map.groupBy()` — keys, prototypes and ordering?
description: Both ES2024 grouping methods look similar but differ in key types and return structures. Learn when to choose each and the performance trade-offs.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="210" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="125" y="85" text-anchor="middle">callback -> key</text><text class="d-sub" x="125" y="105" text-anchor="middle">string / object / ...</text><line class="d-edge" x1="230" y1="65" x2="320" y2="65"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="320,65 310,59 310,71"/><rect class="d-box" x="330" y="10" width="180" height="70" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="420" y="40" text-anchor="middle">Object.groupBy</text><text class="d-sub" x="420" y="58" text-anchor="middle">string/symbol key</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="230" y1="115" x2="320" y2="115"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="320,115 310,109 310,121"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="330" y="95" width="180" height="70" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="420" y="125" text-anchor="middle">Map.groupBy</text><text class="d-sub" x="420" y="143" text-anchor="middle">any key type</text><rect class="d-box-muted" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="80" text-anchor="middle">Choose by key</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="100" text-anchor="middle">JSON vs object key</text></svg>

**Core concept.** Object.groupBy coerces keys to strings/symbols and returns a null-prototype object; Map.groupBy preserves any key type (objects, numbers, NaN) and returns a Map — choose by whether keys must stay non-string.

How it works — Both take (iterable, callback). Object.groupBy is for JSON-friendly, string-keyed results: callback returning 42 and "42" collide, and object keys become "[object Object]". Map.groupBy keeps key identity via SameValueZero (like Map), so 42 stays number, NaN equals NaN, and two distinct objects are distinct keys. That matters when grouping by a reference, e.g., grouping DOM nodes by their parent object.

Ordering also differs subtly: both preserve insertion order of groups, but Map iterates via for...of entries and has .size, while the Object result needs Object.keys and has no size. Map also better supports frequent add/delete and avoids string coercion overhead. For serialization, Object wins — JSON.stringify works directly; Map needs Array.from(map.entries()).

Interviewer trap: Object.groupBy({ length: 2, 0: 'a', 1: 'b' }) does not treat array-like specially — it groups the iterable itself, not array-like. And callback returning undefined/null creates "undefined"/"null" keys in Object but real undefined/null keys in Map.

| | Object.groupBy | Map.groupBy |
|---|---|---|
| Return | null-proto object | Map |
| Key type | string / symbol | any (object, number, NaN) |
| Serialization | JSON ready | Needs conversion |
| Lookup | obj[key] (stringified) | map.get(key) (identity) |

> **Interview tip:** Answer with a collision example: grouping by {} gives one bucket in Object but separate buckets in Map if different references. Say you default to Object for string keys, Map for non-primitives.

```js
const items = [
  { id: 1, c: 'a' }, { id: 2, c: 'a' }, { id: 3, c: 'b' }
];
console.log(Object.groupBy(items, x => x.c)); // { a: [...], b: [...] }
console.log(Map.groupBy(items, x => x.c)); // Map { 'a' => [...], 'b' => [...] }

// key-type difference
const byObj = Object.groupBy([1,2], () => ({}));
console.log(Object.keys(byObj)); // ['[object Object]'] — collision!
const byMap = Map.groupBy([1,2], () => ({}));
console.log(byMap.size); // 1 — same {} ref reused per call? distinct exam:
const keyA = {}, keyB = {};
console.log(Map.groupBy([1,2], v => v===1? keyA : keyB).size); // 2

// numbers vs strings
console.log(Object.groupBy([1,2], x => x)); // { '1': [1], '2': [2] } keys are strings
console.log([...Map.groupBy([1,2], x => x).keys()]); // [1,2] numbers preserved
```

title: What does `Promise.try()` do and why is it better than `Promise.resolve().then(fn)`?
description: Promise.try unifies sync and async errors by running a function and wrapping its result. Learn how it fixes unhandled rejection and execution order pitfalls.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">fn() throws?</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">sync or async</text><line class="d-edge" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Promise.try(fn)</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">wrap -> promise</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Rejected promise</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">never sync throw</text></svg>

**Core concept.** Promise.try(fn) executes fn immediately, catches any synchronous throw as a rejected promise, and awaits thenables — guaranteeing uniform async error handling without subtle then timing.

How it works — Promise.resolve().then(fn) defers fn to a microtask, so a throw inside fn becomes a rejection but fn does not run until the next tick, which can reorder operations and hide stack traces. Promise.try(fn) runs fn synchronously in the current turn and only then wraps the result: if fn returns a value, resolve; if it throws, reject; if it returns a promise, adopt it. Execution is immediate, not enqueued.

This fixes the double-error-handling trap: with try/catch around await you still need to wrap both sync and async paths; Promise.try normalizes them so one .catch handles both. It also avoids the unnecessary extra promise allocation of Promise.resolve().then — engines can optimize the try path.

Use it when bridging callback-style code that may throw synchronously before returning a promise, or when composing pipelines where some steps are sync and some async. It is static like Promise.all.

| | Before (Promise.resolve().then) | After (Promise.try) |
|---|---|---|
| Execution | Deferred to microtask | Immediate, sync run |
| Allocation | Extra intermediate promise | Single promise |
| Stack | Longer async stack | Cleaner, fn frame preserved |
| Nesting | Common to forget | Single wrapper |

> **Interview tip:** Mention the execution-order difference — try is sync, then is async. If asked to implement, show try { return fn() } catch(e) { return Promise.reject(e) } but explain Promise.try also unwraps thenables.

```js
// before — subtle deferral
Promise.resolve().then(() => JSON.parse('bad')); // rejects next tick

// after — immediate but safe
Promise.try(() => JSON.parse('bad')).catch(e => console.log('caught', e.message));

// handles mixed sync/async uniformly
function maybeAsync(x) {
  if (x === 1) throw new Error('sync');
  if (x === 2) return Promise.reject(new Error('async'));
  return 42;
}

Promise.try(() => maybeAsync(1)).catch(e => console.log(e.message)); // sync -> rejection
Promise.try(() => maybeAsync(2)).catch(e => console.log(e.message)); // async -> rejection
Promise.try(() => maybeAsync(3)).then(v => console.log(v)); // 42

// vs try/catch needing two paths
try {
  const v = await Promise.try(() => maybeAsync(3));
} catch(e) { /* one handler for both */ }
```

title: What is `Error.isError()` and why is `instanceof Error` unreliable across realms?
description: Error.isError is the ES2025 robust check for error objects that works across iframes and ShadowRealms where instanceof fails. Learn the cross-realm problem.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">error value</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">from iframe/realm</text><line class="d-edge" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">instanceof Error</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">false (diff realm)</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Error.isError()</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">true — spec check</text></svg>

**Core concept.** Error.isError(value) returns true for any native Error regardless of realm, fixing cross-iframe and ShadowRealm cases where instanceof Error returns false because each realm has its own Error constructor.

How it works — instanceof checks prototype chain against a specific constructor, so new iframe.contentWindow.Error('x') instanceof window.Error is false — different prototype roots. Error.isError uses the spec internal slot [[ErrorData]] to detect error-ness structurally, not by prototype identity. It returns true for Error, TypeError, RangeError, etc., and false for plain objects that merely look like errors { message, name }.

This matters in libraries that catch and rethrow across boundaries: logging, serialization, and error boundaries in micro-frontends. Previously the workaround was Object.prototype.toString.call(e) === '[object Error]' or checking e && typeof e.message === 'string', both fragile. Error.isError is the canonical detector, similar to Array.isArray fixing Array realm issues years earlier.

Note: it does not coerce — Error.isError('oops') is false — and it detects only native errors, not user subclasses that do not call super(). For custom errors, still use instanceof within the same realm or duck-type on .cause.

| | Before (instanceof) | After (Error.isError) |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-realm | false across iframes | true |
| Lookalike {message} | false (correct but brittle) | false (robust) |
| Subclass without super | false | false (needs [[ErrorData]]) |
| Polyfill | toString hack | native spec check |

> **Interview tip:** Bring up Array.isArray as the precedent — both fix the same realm problem. Say you would use Error.isError in a catch-all that decides whether to attach .cause or serialize.

```js
// same-realm
console.log(Error.isError(new TypeError('bad'))); // true
console.log(Error.isError({ message: 'nope', name: 'Error' })); // false

// cross-realm demo (conceptual — iframe has different Error)
const iframe = document.createElement('iframe');
document.body.appendChild(iframe);
const otherErr = iframe.contentWindow.Error('from iframe');
console.log(otherErr instanceof Error); // false — different realm!
console.log(Error.isError(otherErr)); // true

// practical: safe error handling
function logError(e) {
  if (Error.isError(e)) console.error(e.stack);
  else console.error('non-error thrown', e);
}

// polyfill for older engines
if (!Error.isError) Error.isError = v => Object.prototype.toString.call(v) === '[object Error]' || v instanceof Error;
```

title: How does V8 Array copy-on-write optimization work for `toSorted`/`toReversed`/`toSpliced`/`with`?
description: ES2023 non-mutating array methods are optimized via copy-on-write in V8. Understand shallow copy sharing, element kinds, and when a real copy happens.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Original Array</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">backing store</text><line class="d-edge" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">toSorted() COW</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">shared buffer</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Write -> copy</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">on first mutation</text></svg>

**Core concept.** V8 implements toSorted/toReversed/toSpliced/with with copy-on-write: the returned array initially shares the backing store and only materializes a copy on first write, making non-mutating ops near-free for read-heavy flows.

How it works — Naively, toSorted would allocate and copy n elements then sort. Copy-on-write (COW) defers the copy: both arrays point to the same heap backing store with a COW flag. Reads are direct; the moment you write to either array, V8 triggers the actual copy (and element-kind deoptimization if needed). For sorted, the sort necessarily writes, so the copy happens during sort, but for with(2, 99) which changes one element, COW avoids copying the other n-1 unchanged elements until needed, and for chaining e.g., arr.toReversed().toSorted() engines can elide intermediate copies.

Element kinds matter: PACKED_SMI_ELEMENTS vs HOLEY vs PACKED_ELEMENTS. COW arrays start packed if source is packed; writing a hole or an object transitions kinds. Interviewers probe why arr[1000000]=1 deoptimizes — because it creates holes. toSpliced on a holey array propagates holes cheaply via COW without scanning.

Implication: prefer the non-mutating variants in Redux-style immutable updates — they are not slower than manual slice+mutate; often faster. They also guarantee the original is untouched, simplifying reasoning.

| | Before (slice + sort) | After (toSorted COW) |
|---|---|---|
| Allocation | Eager full copy | Lazy, shared initially |
| Memory | 2x during copy | ~1x until write |
| Chaining | Each step copies | Can share/optimize |
| Holes | Copies holes eagerly | Lazy hole handling |

> **Interview tip:** Mention PACKED vs HOLEY and that toSorted is the idiomatic immutable sort — in interviews replace [...arr].sort() with arr.toSorted() and justify with COW.

```js
const arr = [3,1,2];
const sorted = arr.toSorted((a,b)=>a-b);
console.log(arr); // [3,1,2] untouched
console.log(sorted); // [1,2,3]

// with — single element change, COW cheap
const base = Array.from({length: 100000}, (_,i)=>i);
console.time('with');
const changed = base.with(50000, 999999);
console.timeEnd('with'); // ~microseconds due to COW

// toSpliced — no mutation
const spliced = [1,2,3,4].toSpliced(1,2, 9, 9);
console.log(spliced); // [1,9,9,4]

// holey case
const holey = [1,,3]; // holey
console.log(holey.toReversed()); // [3, empty, 1] — holes preserved
```

title: What does the RegExp `v` flag (Unicode Sets) add over the `u` flag?
description: The v flag upgrades regex to set-notation, intersection and nested properties. Learn why emoji and string-class matching now works correctly.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">/\p{Emoji}/u</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">single char only</text><line class="d-edge" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">/--v flag</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">sets + intersect</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">[\p{Emoji}&&\q{}]</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">multi-char strings</text></svg>

**Core concept.** The v flag enables Unicode Set Notation — set operations (&& intersection, -- difference), nested classes, and string literals (\q{}) for correct multi-codepoint emoji matching that u cannot handle.

How it works — u gives Unicode-aware mode where \p{Property} works but only for single codepoints; emoji like 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 are sequences joined by ZWJ, so /\p{Emoji}/u matches each codepoint separately and breaks. v upgrades the parser to a Unicode Sets level: you can write [\p{Emoji}--\p{ASCII}] (emoji minus ASCII), [A&&B] intersections, and double-punctuator [\[ -- ]] without escaping, plus \q{AB|CD} to match literal strings inside a character class context.

Internally, v also fixes case-folding and property escapes for extended graphemes and makes character classes composable. v is a superset of u behavior — enabling v implies u semantics plus sets. They are mutually exclusive flags (cannot use both). Browsers ship v in Chrome 112+, Firefox 116+, and Node 20+; transpilers will not polyfill it because it changes parsing.

Practical use: validate that a username contains only letters minus confusables: /^[\p{Letter}&&[^\p{ASCII}]]+$/v or strip emoji ZWJ sequences correctly.

| | Before (u) | After (v) |
|---|---|---|
| Set ops | No — manual ranges | &&, --, nested [] |
| Multi-char emoji | Breaks ZWJ sequences | \q{👨‍👩‍👧|👨‍👩‍👧‍👦} works |
| Escaping | Must escape ] ^ - | Cleaner due to set notation |
| Compat | Wide | Chrome 112+ / Node 20+ |

> **Interview tip:** Say "v fixes emoji sequences — u cannot match \q strings" and show an intersection example. Interviewers test if you know v replaces u, not adds to it.

```js
// u — breaks ZWJ emoji
const reU = /\p{Emoji}/u;
console.log('👨‍👩‍👧'.match(reU)); // matches single codepoint fragment

// v — string literal and set difference
const reV = /^[\p{Emoji}--\p{ASCII}]+$/v;
console.log(reV.test('hello')); // false (ASCII removed)
console.log(reV.test('😀👍')); // true

// intersection
const lettersNonAscii = /[\p{Letter}&&[^\p{ASCII}]]/v;
console.log(lettersNonAscii.test('é')); // true
console.log(lettersNonAscii.test('a')); // false

// \q — match exact strings inside set context
const family = /\q{👨‍👩‍👧|👨‍👩‍👧‍👦}/v;
console.log('👨‍👩‍👧‍👦'.match(family));

// difference — emoji minus digits
const emojiNoDigits = /[\p{Emoji}--[0-9]]/v;
```

title: How do the new Set methods `union()`, `intersection()`, `difference()` and `symmetricDifference()` work?
description: ES2024+ adds native Set algebra. Learn the four core methods, their symmetry, and when they beat manual loops for performance.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="180" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="110" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Set A {1,2,3}</text><text class="d-sub" x="110" y="105" text-anchor="middle">size 3</text><rect class="d-box" x="220" y="40" width="180" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="310" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Set B {3,4,5}</text><text class="d-sub" x="310" y="105" text-anchor="middle">size 3</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="400" y1="65" x2="480" y2="65"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="480,65 470,59 470,71"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="500" y="10" width="140" height="60" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="570" y="40" text-anchor="middle">A.union(B)</text><text class="d-sub" x="570" y="55" text-anchor="middle">{1,2,3,4,5}</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="400" y1="115" x2="480" y2="115"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="480,115 470,109 470,121"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="500" y="100" width="140" height="60" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="570" y="130" text-anchor="middle">A.intersect(B)</text><text class="d-sub" x="570" y="145" text-anchor="middle">{3}</text></svg>

**Core concept.** ES2024 adds set algebra: union (all), intersection (common), difference (A minus B), symmetricDifference (either but not both) — each returns a new Set without mutating inputs.

How it works — All four are instance methods: a.union(b), a.intersection(b), a.difference(b), a.symmetricDifference(b). Arguments can be any Set-like (iterable of unique values). They use SameValueZero semantics like Set.has, so NaN equals NaN and +0 equals -0. Each returns a new Set, leaving originals untouched, which fits immutable patterns.

Performance is engine-optimized: union iterates smaller set first; intersection tracks via hash table O(n+m) without userland loops. Still O(n) memory for results. Additional helpers isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf, and isDisjointFrom return booleans without allocating a new set, useful for permission checks: roles.isSupersetOf(required).

Common pitfall: union of objects uses reference identity, not deep equality — {a:1} in setA and new {a:1} in setB are distinct. And all methods create new Sets, so chaining a.union(b).intersection(c) allocates intermediaries; for hot paths, consider manual single-pass via loop.

| | Before (manual) | After (native) |
|---|---|---|
| Union | new Set([...a, ...b]) | a.union(b) — handles duplicates, optimized |
| Intersection | [...a].filter(x=>b.has(x)) | a.intersection(b) — O(n), no intermediate array |
| Difference | [...a].filter(x=>!b.has(x)) | a.difference(b) |
| Subset test | every check loop | a.isSubsetOf(b) — no allocation |

> **Interview tip:** Mention SameValueZero and that methods return new Sets (immutable). Show isDisjointFrom for fast early-exit without building a set.

```js
const a = new Set([1,2,3]);
const b = new Set([3,4,5]);

console.log(a.union(b)); // Set {1,2,3,4,5}
console.log(a.intersection(b)); // Set {3}
console.log(a.difference(b)); // Set {1,2}
console.log(a.symmetricDifference(b)); // Set {1,2,4,5}

console.log(a.isSubsetOf(new Set([1,2,3,4]))); // true
console.log(a.isDisjointFrom(new Set([4,5]))); // true
console.log(a.isSupersetOf(new Set([2]))); // true

// real: permission check
const userPerms = new Set(['read','write']);
const required = new Set(['read']);
console.log(userPerms.isSupersetOf(required)); // true

// pitfall — object identity
const o1 = {}, o2 = {};
new Set([o1]).union(new Set([o2])).size // 2, not 1
```

title: How do Stage 3 JavaScript Decorators work — class, method and field decorators?
description: Stage 3 decorators are functions that wrap classes and members at define-time. Learn the new single-function form and how it differs from TypeScript legacy decorators.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">@decorator</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">declaration</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Wrap descriptor</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">value / getter / class</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">New behavior</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">memo, bound, logged</text></svg>

**Core concept.** Stage 3 decorators are plain functions called at class-definition time that receive the target and a context object, returning a replacement — unified for classes, methods, accessors and fields.

How it works — You write @logged class Foo {} or @bound method() {}. The decorator is invoked once when the class is defined, not per instance. Signature: function decorator(target, context) where context.kind is 'class' | 'method' | 'getter' | 'field' | 'accessor', plus name, metadata, and addInitializer hook. Returning a new function/class or descriptor replacement changes the definition. Unlike legacy TypeScript experimental decorators (3 args, prototype hacks), Stage 3 uses a single call and no descriptor mutation — cleaner and composable.

Order matters: decorators apply bottom-up (closest to member first), then class decorator, like function composition. Field decorators can inject initializers via context.addInitializer(() => ...). Accessor decorators wrap get/set together, enabling patterns like @memo.

Use cases: @frozen to Object.freeze class, @bound to auto-bind this, @memo to cache getters. Metadata proposal pairs with decorators via Symbol.metadata and context.metadata for reflection.

| | Before (legacy TS) | After (Stage 3) |
|---|---|---|
| Signature | (target, key, descriptor) 3 args | (value, context) 2 args |
| Evaluation | Prototype assignment | Single define-time wrap |
| Field | Not supported cleanly | addInitializer supported |
| Interop | Needs emitDecoratorMetadata | Symbol.metadata |

> **Interview tip:** Point out legacy vs Stage 3 difference — interviewers test if you know they are incompatible. Demo a method decorator that replaces value with a bound wrapper.

```js
// Stage 3 — run with Babel @babel/plugin-proposal-decorators or TS 5.4+ alpha
function bound(target, { kind }) {
  if (kind === 'method') {
    return function(...args) { return target.call(this, ...args); };
  }
}

function logged(Class, { name }) {
  return class extends Class {
    constructor(...a) { console.log('creating', name); super(...a); }
  };
}

function memo(get, { kind }) {
  if (kind === 'getter') {
    const cache = new WeakMap();
    return function() {
      if (cache.has(this)) return cache.get(this);
      const v = get.call(this);
      cache.set(this, v);
      return v;
    };
  }
}

@logged
class Service {
  @memo
  get data() { return { heavy: true }; }

  @bound
  handle() { return this; }
}
console.log(new Service().handle() instanceof Service);
```

title: What is ShadowRealm and how does it provide true JavaScript sandboxing?
description: ShadowRealm is a Stage 3 API for isolated JS evaluation with its own globals. Learn how it differs from iframes, vm, and why it matters for plugins.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box-accent" x="20" y="20" width="360" height="140" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="200" y="50" text-anchor="middle">Main Realm</text><text class="d-sub" x="200" y="70" text-anchor="middle">window, Array.prototype</text><rect class="d-box" x="60" y="80" width="120" height="60" rx="10"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="110" text-anchor="middle">Your code</text><rect class="d-box-muted" x="220" y="80" width="120" height="60" rx="10"/><text class="d-text" x="280" y="110" text-anchor="middle">ShadowRealm</text><text class="d-sub" x="280" y="125" text-anchor="middle">own globals</text><line class="d-edge-dashed" x1="180" y1="110" x2="220" y2="110"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="220,110 210,104 210,116"/><rect class="d-box" x="500" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="600" y="80" text-anchor="middle">evaluate(code)</text><text class="d-sub" x="600" y="100" text-anchor="middle">wrapped func only</text><text class="d-sub" x="600" y="115" text-anchor="middle">no DOM access</text></svg>

**Core concept.** ShadowRealm creates a fresh JavaScript realm with its own globals and intrinsics, letting you evaluate untrusted code in isolation without iframe overhead and without sharing prototypes.

How it works — new ShadowRealm() constructs an empty global environment: its own Array, Object, Error, etc., with no DOM, no window, no access to outer variables. You run code via realm.evaluate('1+2') or wrap functions via realm.importValue(specifier, binding). The caller and the realm can only exchange wrapped functions — primitives are copied, objects are wrapped as callable proxies with no prototype leakage. That guarantees prototype pollution in the sandbox does not affect the main realm.

Contrast with old sandboxing: iframes share DOM and are heavy; Node vm still shares intrinsics by default; eval has full access. ShadowRealm is the only built-in that gives true global isolation specified by TC39. It does not provide async import yet (importValue is async) and cannot access host DOM, so it is for logic plugins, template evaluation, and AI-generated code execution.

Error handling propagates via wrapped errors — caught in the main realm they appear as TypeErrors unless unwrapped. A module loader can expose vetted globals by injecting bindings before evaluate.

| | Before (iframe / eval) | After (ShadowRealm) |
|---|---|---|
| Globals | Shared or heavy iframe | Fresh, lightweight |
| DOM | Accessible | No DOM, safe |
| Prototype pollution | Leaks to main | Isolated |
| Communication | postMessage / direct | Wrapped functions only |

> **Interview tip:** Say "ShadowRealm is not a DOM sandbox — it has no window or document by design." Contrast with Worker and iframe + mention wrapped function bridging is the only channel.

```js
const realm = new ShadowRealm();

// isolated evaluation — cannot see outer let
let x = 42;
console.log(realm.evaluate('typeof x')); // 'undefined' — isolated
console.log(realm.evaluate('1 + 2')); // 3

// own intrinsics — pollution does not leak
realm.evaluate('Array.prototype.push = () => "hacked"');
console.log([1,2].push(3)); // 3 (unchanged)

// wrap a function to bridge realms
const wrapped = realm.evaluate('(x) => x * 2');
console.log(typeof wrapped); // function (wrapped)
// wrapped call executes inside realm but is callable from main
console.log(wrapped(21)); // 42

// async import (proposed)
// const mod = await realm.importValue('./plugin.mjs', 'handler');
// mod() runs inside realm
```

title: How does `Atomics.waitAsync()` enable non-blocking waits on SharedArrayBuffer?
description: Atomics.wait blocks the thread; waitAsync returns a promise that resolves when notified. Learn the async coordination pattern for workers.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="180" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="110" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Main thread</text><text class="d-sub" x="110" y="105" text-anchor="middle">await waitAsync</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="200" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="280,90 270,84 270,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="290" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="390" y="85" text-anchor="middle">SharedArrayBuffer</text><text class="d-sub" x="390" y="105" text-anchor="middle">Int32Array[0]</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="490" y1="90" x2="570" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="570,90 560,84 560,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="580" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="680" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Worker notifies</text><text class="d-sub" x="680" y="105" text-anchor="middle">promise resolves</text></svg>

**Core concept.** Atomics.waitAsync lets the main thread wait on a SharedArrayBuffer location without blocking, returning { async: true, value: Promise } that resolves on notify, unlike Atomics.wait which blocks and is forbidden on the main thread.

How it works — SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics coordinate workers. Atomics.wait(i32, index, value, timeout) blocks the calling thread until another thread calls Atomics.notify. That blocking is illegal on the main thread (would freeze UI) and throws. waitAsync solves it: if the current value already differs, it returns { async: false, value: 'not-equal' } synchronously; otherwise it returns { async: true, value: promise } where the promise resolves to 'ok' or 'timed-out' upon notification. You await the promise without blocking the event loop.

Pattern: main thread creates new SharedArrayBuffer(4), wraps Int32Array, spawns a worker, then await Atomics.waitAsync(i32, 0, 0).value before updating UI. Worker does heavy work then Atomics.store(i32, 0, 1) + Atomics.notify(i32, 0, 1). This is the primitive behind WASM threading and high-performance worker pools.

Timeout variant allows polling without busy-wait: waitAsync with 1000 ms timeout yields 'timed-out' if not notified, letting you implement graceful fallback.

| | Before (Atomics.wait) | After (waitAsync) |
|---|---|---|
| Main thread | Throws (blocking) | Non-blocking promise |
| Return | 'ok' string sync | {async, value: Promise} |
| Use site | Workers only | Main + workers |
| UI | Would freeze | Event loop stays free |

> **Interview tip:** Emphasize that wait is illegal on window — interviewers test that. Say you always check result.async before awaiting, handling the sync not-equal fast path.

```js
// main thread — non-blocking wait
const sab = new SharedArrayBuffer(4);
const i32 = new Int32Array(sab);
i32[0] = 0;

async function waitForWorker() {
  const res = Atomics.waitAsync(i32, 0, 0);
  if (!res.async) {
    console.log('already changed:', res.value); // not-equal
    return;
  }
  console.log('waiting...');
  const outcome = await res.value; // 'ok' or 'timed-out'
  console.log('woke:', outcome);
}

// worker.js — heavy work then notify
// Atomics.store(i32, 0, 1);
// Atomics.notify(i32, 0, 1);

// with timeout
const r = Atomics.waitAsync(i32, 0, 0, 1000);
if (r.async) {
  r.value.then(v => console.log(v === 'timed-out' ? 'timeout' : 'notified'));
}

// fallback for older engines
if (!Atomics.waitAsync) {
  // poll — worse but works on main
  Atomics.wait = undefined; // would throw on main anyway
}
```

title: Temporal in practice: how do you correctly handle time zones, DST and calendar arithmetic?
description: Beyond basics, Temporal solves real scheduling bugs around DST gaps and month-length math. Learn practical patterns for booking and billing systems.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="220" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="130" y="85" text-anchor="middle">PlainDateTime</text><text class="d-sub" x="130" y="105" text-anchor="middle">2025-03-09 02:30 ?</text><line class="d-edge-dashed" x1="240" y1="90" x2="320" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="320,90 310,84 310,96"/><rect class="d-box-muted" x="330" y="40" width="180" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="420" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Gap (DST)</text><text class="d-sub" x="420" y="105" text-anchor="middle">does not exist</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">ZonedDateTime</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">03:30 -04:00 ok</text></svg>

**Core concept.** For scheduling use ZonedDateTime with disambiguation options; for arithmetic use add with overflow control — this handles DST gaps where 02:30 does not exist and months with varying lengths.

How it works — DST creates nonexistent and ambiguous wall times. On 2025-03-09 in America/New_York, clocks jump 02:00→03:00, so 02:30 is invalid. PlainDateTime lets you represent it but converting to ZonedDateTime requires disambiguation: compatible (jumps forward), earlier, later, or reject. Temporal defaults to compatible, pushing 02:30 to 03:30, but booking systems should use reject to surface the error.

Month arithmetic is calendar-aware, not fixed days. PlainDate.from('2025-01-31').add({ months: 1 }) yields 2025-02-28 (constrain overflow), not March 3. With overflow: 'reject' it throws; with 'balance' it overflows to next month. Billing that charges monthly must use constrain and document it. Duration total() with relativeTo lets you compute exact hours between zoned instants, accounting for DST length changes (23 or 25-hour days).

Immutability and explicit zones make these choices visible; Date hides them and yields off-by-one hour bugs that only appear twice a year.

| | Before (Date) | After (Temporal ZDT) |
|---|---|---|
| DST gap | Silent 03:30 shift | Disambiguation choice |
| Month add | Fixed 30 days | Calendar-aware |
| Ambiguous fall-back | Duplicate 01:30 | earlier/later option |
| Precision | ms, drift | ns, exact |

> **Interview tip:** Say "never add 24*60*60*1000 for days — use add({days:1}) on a ZonedDateTime." Mention disambiguation modes by name.

```js
// DST gap — March 9 2025 NY
const bad = Temporal.PlainDateTime.from('2025-03-09T02:30:00');
try {
  bad.toZonedDateTime('America/New_York', { disambiguation: 'reject' });
} catch(e) { console.log('gap rejected', e.message); }

const ok = bad.toZonedDateTime('America/New_York', { disambiguation: 'compatible' });
console.log(ok.toString()); // 2025-03-09T03:30:00-04:00[America/New_York]

// month arithmetic
const jan31 = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2025-01-31');
console.log(jan31.add({ months: 1 }).toString()); // 2025-02-28 (constrain)
try { jan31.add({ months: 1 }, { overflow: 'reject' }); } catch(e){ console.log('reject overflow'); }

// exact duration across DST
const start = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from('2025-03-08T12:00:00[America/New_York]');
const end = start.add({ days: 1 });
console.log(start.until(end).total({ unit: 'hours' })); // 23 — spring forward
```

title: Set methods deep-dive: performance and mutability trade-offs vs manual loops?
description: Beyond syntax, understand when native Set methods outperform manual spread+filter, memory churn of chaining, and SameValueZero edge cases.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Loop + has()</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">O(n) + intermediaries</text><line class="d-edge" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Native .intersection</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">hash-opt, no array</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">No allocation*</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">isDisjointFrom</text></svg>

**Core concept.** Native Set methods are hash-table optimized and avoid intermediate arrays, but they always return new Sets — chaining creates allocations; for hot paths, single-pass manual loops or isDisjointFrom can be faster.

How it works — [...a].filter(x => b.has(x)) creates an intermediate array, then new Set(...), doubling iteration and memory. Native intersection directly builds a Set from the smaller input while probing the larger hash table, no array. For 100k elements, native is ~2-3× faster in V8 microbenchmarks and generates less GC pressure.

Mutability: all Set algebra returns a fresh Set, preserving immutability semantics important for React state. If you need in-place mutation for performance, you must write it manually: for (const v of b) if (!a.has(v)) ... But then you break purity. The boolean trio isSubsetOf/isSupersetOf/isDisjointFrom exists precisely to avoid allocation when you only need a predicate.

Edge: SameValueZero means NaN matches NaN and -0 === +0, consistent with Set.has. For object elements, identity matters, so intersection of sets of {id} objects is nearly always empty unless references share. Large union of two 1M sets transiently holds ~2M entries — consider streaming or chunking.

| | Before (manual) | After (native) |
|---|---|---|
| Allocations | Array + Set | Single Set |
| Speed | O(n) + GC | Hash-optimized, less GC |
| Predicate check | Filter then length | isDisjointFrom (no alloc) |
| Readability | 3-step | One method call |

> **Interview tip:** Say "native methods avoid intermediate arrays but still allocate — for boolean checks use isSubsetOf to avoid building a set at all." Mention SameValueZero.

```js
// manual — extra allocation
function intersectManual(a,b){
  return new Set([...a].filter(x=> b.has(x)));
}

// native — no intermediate array
const a = new Set(Array.from({length: 100000}, (_,i)=>i));
const b = new Set(Array.from({length: 100000}, (_,i)=>i+50000));
console.time('native');
a.intersection(b);
console.timeEnd('native');

// predicate without allocation
console.log(a.isDisjointFrom(new Set([999999]))); // true — no set built

// chaining cost — two allocations
const c = new Set([1,2,3]);
const chained = a.union(b).intersection(c); // 2 new Sets

// in-place for hot path (mutates)
function unionInto(target, source){
  for (const v of source) target.add(v);
  return target;
}
```

title: How do you combine Stage 3 decorators with `using` for auto-disposable resources?
description: Decorators can register disposal and metadata while `using` guarantees cleanup. Learn the DisposableStack + decorator pattern for files and observers.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box-accent" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">@disposable</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">class + Symbol.dispose</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">instance</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">auto cleanup logic</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">using res = new R()</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">LIFO dispose</text></svg>

**Core concept.** A @disposable class decorator injects [Symbol.dispose] and registers the instance with metadata, while using guarantees the dispose runs on scope exit — decorators handle how, using handles when.

How it works — Decorators run at define time and can attach disposal behavior without boilerplate in each class. Example: @tracked adds [Symbol.dispose] that removes event listeners and logs via context.metadata. The instance itself carries no manual close call; the consumer simply writes using res = new Resource(). When the block exits, the engine calls res[Symbol.dispose] even if the consumer forgot or threw.

This composes with DisposableStack for conditional resources: the decorator can push the instance onto a stack via context.addInitializer, and using stack ensures grouped cleanup in LIFO order. Async variant @asyncDisposable with Symbol.asyncDispose pairs with await using for DB connections.

Metadata proposal enhances this: context.metadata lets decorators stash cleanup priorities or ownership tags, inspected by devtools. Without using, decorators alone cannot enforce timing — without decorators, using requires manual Symbol.dispose on each class. Together they give RAII with declarative intent.

| | Before (manual close) | After (decorator + using) |
|---|---|---|
| Boilerplate | close() in every class + try/finally | One decorator, zero consumer boilerplate |
| Safety | Forgotten close | Guaranteed on throw/return |
| Grouping | Manual array of handles | DisposableStack + using |
| Observability | Ad-hoc | metadata for tooling |

> **Interview tip:** Say "decorators define disposable contract, using enforces it." Show that decorator can wrap dispose with try/catch and emit SuppressedError handling.

```js
// decorator that makes a class disposable
function disposable(Class, { metadata }) {
  const orig = Class.prototype[Symbol.dispose];
  Class.prototype[Symbol.dispose] = function() {
    console.log('disposing', this.id);
    orig?.call(this);
  };
  return Class;
}

@disposable
class FileHandle {
  constructor(id){ this.id = id; }
  [Symbol.dispose](){ console.log('close', this.id); }
}

{
  using fh = new FileHandle('a');
  console.log('using', fh.id);
} // using a -> close a -> disposing a

// async + decorator
function asyncDisposable(Class){
  Class.prototype[Symbol.asyncDispose] = async function(){ console.log('async close'); };
  return Class;
}
@asyncDisposable
class Conn {}
async function demo(){
  await using c = new Conn();
  console.log('query');
} // query -> async close

// with stack for dynamic resources
{
  using stack = new DisposableStack();
  stack.use(new FileHandle('b'));
  if (Math.random() > 0.5) stack.use(new FileHandle('c'));
} // LIFO dispose b then c if created
```
